title: Find pairs of employees who have the same salary (across the whole list).
shortTitle: Find pairs of employees who have the same salary (across the whole list)

s1_definition.profdef: You group employees by salary, keep groups with more than one member, and from each such group enumerate the pairs of employees sharing that salary.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya groups people by their pay, finds the pay levels with two or more people, and lists the pairs who earn the same.
s1_definition.oneliner: Group by salary, keep groups of size > 1, then form pairs within each group.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You group employees by salary, keep groups with more than one member, and from each such group enumerate the pairs of employees sharing that salary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya groups people by their pay, finds the pay levels with two or more people, and lists the pairs who earn the same.

**One line to remember:** Group by salary, keep groups of size > 1, then form pairs within each group.

sections.s2_technical:
`groupingBy(Employee::getSalary)` buckets employees by salary into `Map<BigDecimal, List<Employee>>`. You filter to groups with more than one member, then for each such group enumerate pairs with nested index loops: for i from 0 to size and j from i plus one, pair element i with element j. Collecting these gives all same-salary pairs.

Grouping first is the key efficiency: it avoids comparing every employee against every other (O(n²)); you only form pairs within groups that actually share a salary. For BigDecimal salaries, grouping uses equals, so I normalise scale or use a comparison-friendly key to avoid scale mismatches.

The senior nuance is the pair enumeration being quadratic only within each shared group, not across the whole list, which is far cheaper when few salaries collide. I decide pair ordering and whether (A,B) and (B,A) are the same pair — usually yes, so the j-starts-at-i-plus-one loop avoids duplicates and self-pairs. BigDecimal equality by scale is a subtle correctness point for money keys.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A pay-audit at the National Bank of India lists pairs of employees earning identical salaries to review for parity.

This is exactly what group-by-salary then pair-within-group does — it produces same-salary pairs efficiently.

The code defines a `PayAuditService.sameSalaryPairs method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh, Amit, Priya all at 800,000 and Neha at 600,000.

Step 1: Grouping by salary buckets Rajesh, Amit, Priya under 800,000 and Neha alone under 600,000.

Step 2: The size filter keeps only the 800,000 group since it has three members.

Step 3: The nested loop forms the unique pairs within that group: Rajesh-Amit, Rajesh-Priya, Amit-Priya.

Step 4: Neha's singleton group yields no pairs.

```
INFO: Rajesh & Amit share a salary
INFO: Rajesh & Priya share a salary
INFO: Amit & Priya share a salary
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [Rajesh/800k, Amit/800k, Priya/800k, Neha/600k]
    │ groupingBy(salary) → {800k=[Rajesh, Amit, Priya], 600k=[Neha]}
    │ keep groups size > 1 → 800k group
    │ pairs: (i, j>i) within group
    ▼
  [(Rajesh,Amit), (Rajesh,Priya), (Amit,Priya)]
```

```

  ┌─ group then pair within group ─────────────────────────────┐
  │ groupingBy(salary) → Map<BigDecimal, List<Employee>>       │

  │ BigDecimal key: normalise scale (equals is scale-sensitive) │

  2. for groups size>1: nested (i, j>i) pairs
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To find pairs of employees earning the same salary I first group everyone by salary, then keep only the groups that have more than one member, and within each such group I enumerate the pairs using a nested loop where the inner index starts one past the outer. That produces every unique same-salary pair without self-pairs or duplicates. At the National Bank of India this backs a pay audit that reviews identical salaries for parity.

Grouping first is the efficiency insight. A naive approach compares every employee against every other, which is quadratic across the whole list, whereas grouping means I only form pairs within the groups that actually share a salary, so the quadratic cost applies only inside each shared group rather than across all n employees — a big saving when few salaries collide.

The senior point I stress is BigDecimal as a map key: equals on BigDecimal is scale-sensitive, so eight hundred thousand with two decimal places would not match the same amount with none. I normalise the scale or use a comparison-friendly key so salaries that are numerically equal group together. I also decide explicitly that an unordered pair of A and B is the same as B and A, which the j-starts-at-i-plus-one loop naturally enforces.
